Lab 5: Ship a Feature Through the Pod

Investigate, migrate, extend, and document a real feature using a five role pod.

Block Shipping a Feature
Ticket WM-114 + WM-118
Time 11:00 – 12:30
Where Lab 5 Fits
From one fix on one file to a full feature, through five roles

Recap · Lab 4

BuiltA three role pod (implementer, test-author, contract-reviewer) shipped one fix, on one file, against a failing test.
GapEvery role was pre-built and project scoped. Scope, ownership, and the hand-off between roles were never your call.

This lab · Lab 5

NewAuthor two roles yourself, then carry three forward from Lab 4. Staff a five role pod across two tickets.
NewRun a full feature lifecycle: investigate the blast radius, migrate existing code, extend it, document what moved.
11:00 – 12:30 · Learning Objectives

After This Lab, You Will Be Able To...

  • Run the Read, Decide, Act, Observe loop twice on one feature, once per ticket, and explain why each pass hands off to a different role.
  • Staff a pod across repos: author roles at personal scope, carry roles forward at project scope, and justify the difference as distribution, not capability.
  • Map a change's blast radius before editing: name direct callers, transitive callers, and what a change provably does not reach.
  • Migrate code safely across files in dependency order, and catch over-migration: a signature changed that never needed to change.
  • Originate tests from a ticket before any implementation exists, and treat a checker as a floor, not the spec.
  • Decide when a role does not apply to a ticket, and defend that omission as a deliberate choice.
11:00 – 12:30 · The Pattern

The Same Loop, Twice

Read, Decide, Act, Observe doesn't change today. It just runs twice, once per ticket, with a different role doing the work each pass.

Read

→

Decide

→

Act

→

Observe

→
PhaseWM-114: investigate + migrateWM-118: extend + document
ReadSkim six files. Delegate to impact-mapper for direct, transitive, and not-reached callers.Reframe the ticket. Read the stub's docstring: the only spec that exists.
DecideMigration order, what happens with missing history, what must not change.What "changed" means for a trade whose amount moved but symbol and action didn't.
Actimplementer migrates all six files, bottom up.test-author writes tests from your brief. implementer builds against them.
Observecontract-reviewer reviews the diff. release-scribe writes the note.contract-reviewer reviews the build. A checker confirms the floor.
11:00 – 12:30 · Designing the Pod

Deciding What Belongs in the Pod

Five roles isn't a headcount. Each one exists for a specific, citable reason.

  • One job per role, not one role per teammate
  • Separation of concerns: the writer isn't the grader
  • Isolate verbose work before it floods the main context
  • Least privilege by design, not a cleanup pass
  • Complexity only when it earns its place
"Find the simplest solution possible, and only increase complexity when needed."
Anthropic · Building Effective Agents
11:00 – 12:30 · The Limits

Where Multi-Agent Breaks Down

"Most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research… domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit."

Anthropic · How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System

  • Heavy dependencies between steps: stay serial
  • Shared context needed: stay one role
  • Six files, one working tree: reads parallelize, edits don't
  • WM-118 changes no signature: no map needed
  • A role earns its place. It isn't owed one
11:00 – 12:30 · The Pod

Meet the Pod: Five Roles, Two Tickets

Two roles you author. Three you carry forward from Lab 4. No role works every ticket, and that's by design.

RoleWM-114WM-118
impact-mapperMaps the blast radius before anyone editsNot used
release-scribeWrites the impact noteNot used
implementerMigrates all six filesBuilds the new function
test-authorNot usedWrites the tests from scratch
contract-reviewerReviews the migrationReviews the build
Tool-enforced vs. contract-only: a tool-enforced role literally cannot hold the tool that would let it cheat. A contract-only role is told what not to do in prose. Both labels travel with a role when it's copied; copying a role never changes its contract.
11:00 – 12:30 · Staffing the Pod

Two Roles You Write. Three You Carry Forward.

A project-scoped role doesn't follow you into a new repo on its own. A personal-scoped role already has.

Authored here

impact-mapper (personal) and release-scribe (project) get written from a contract in ROLES.md. Nothing to copy.

Carried forward

implementer, test-author, and contract-reviewer are project-scoped in Lab 4. They exist here only once you copy the files.

Bringing the three project-scoped roles forward

mkdir -p .claude/agents
cp ../lab-4-subagent-pod-intro/.claude/agents/implementer.md .claude/agents/
cp ../lab-4-subagent-pod-intro/.claude/agents/test-author.md .claude/agents/
cp ../lab-4-subagent-pod-intro/.claude/agents/contract-reviewer.md .claude/agents/
impact-mapper needed none of this. The moment you author it at personal scope, it's usable in every project on your machine. That's the friction personal scope buys you out of.
11:00 – 12:30 · The Scope Decision

Personal vs. Project Scope: a Distribution Decision

Same isolated context and enforced tools either way. What differs is who else has the role, and where its cost lands.

Personal: impact-mapper

  • Tracing callers is a habit worth having in every codebase, not a rule about this one.
  • Judgment that stays useful outside this repo's domain and conventions.
  • Loaded in every session on your machine, this project included.

Project: implementer, test-author, contract-reviewer

  • Contracts specific to this repo's tickets and this repo's fee and pricing logic.
  • Checked in, reviewed, and improved by the team that owns the code.
  • Don't travel to a new repo without a copy.
Rule of thumb: if this subagent's description still makes sense in a completely different codebase, it belongs at ~/.claude/agents/. If it only makes sense here, it belongs in the project's .claude/agents/.
11:00 – 12:30 · Authoring a Subagent

Anatomy of a Subagent

Four fields in the frontmatter decide whether Claude Code ever reaches for it.

- - -

name

The identifier you or Claude invoke explicitly: what you'd type after @ to call it directly.

- - -

description

What makes auto-discovery work. Write it like a function signature a router has to match: specific and task-shaped, not generic.

- - -

tools

A least-privilege allowlist. impact-mapper gets Read, Grep, Glob only. release-scribe gets Read, Write, no Edit, so a doc pass can't become a code pass.

- - -

model

The tier the job actually needs, not the strongest one by default.

Rule of thumb

Write the description like a router match. Get it specific and Claude reaches for the subagent on its own; get it vague, and it just does the work inline instead.

11:00 – 12:30 · Ticket 1

WM-114: Investigate + Migrate

Advisors need to reissue a client statement as of a prior date. get_price only returns today's price. One parameter, six files, and two of them never mention pricing at all.

The blast radius

current_weights, compute_trades, and advisory_fee call get_price directly. check_drift and build_statement depend on it transitively, with no pricing anywhere in their own bodies.

The work

impact-mapper maps it and release-scribe documents it. implementer migrates all six files bottom up. contract-reviewer checks for over-migration.

Your goal for WM-114

Map the blast radius, migrate all six files without breaking a single existing caller, and ship impact_note.md naming every call site check_impact_note.py expects.

11:00 – 12:30 · Investigate

Direct, Transitive, Not Reached

A grep finds the three direct callers. impact-mapper earns its place on the other two rows.

FunctionDepends on get_priceClassification
current_weightsCalls it directly, for each position's market valueDirect
compute_tradesCalls it directly, to plan tradesDirect
advisory_feeCalls it directly, to value the bookDirect
check_driftVia current_weights, never calls it itselfTransitive
build_statementNever mentions pricing in its own bodyTransitive
target_weightsA static profile, no pricing at allNot affected
A map that stops at direct callers is wrong, not incomplete. A migration planned off it tells the advisor team the wrong thing is safe.
11:00 – 12:30 · Migrate

Three Decisions Before the First Edit

The map tells you what to touch. It doesn't tell you how. Decide these before briefing the implementer.

Order

Bottom up, in dependency order. A failure then names the layer that broke it, instead of hiding six layers deep.

Semantics the ticket skips

A date with no end-of-day mark. A date before the history begins. The contract answers both, read it before writing code.

What must not change

Every existing caller still gets today's answer. That's why as_of_date defaults to None, never to a computed today.

The trap: compute_trades reaches pricing twice. Forward the date to one call site and trades land on the right symbol, right direction, wrong amount. One test catches it. A human reviewer likely wouldn't.
11:00 – 12:30 · The Silent Failure

Over-Migration Has No Error Message

Every migration has two ways to be wrong. Teams only ever guard against the first.

A caller you missed

Loud. A test fails, you fix it, done. This is the failure mode everyone plans for.

A caller you changed that didn't need it

Silent. Every test passes. You've permanently added a parameter no caller can vary, and the next engineer has to work out why.

target_weights has no pricing in it, directly or transitively. Threading the date through it passes every test. Only a reviewer with an explicit criterion, every signature that changed needed to change, ever catches it.
11:00 – 12:30 · Separation of Concerns

Two Jobs, One Role: Repair vs. Originate

A test-authoring role does two different jobs. Neither one belongs to the role writing the implementation.

Repair

A change made a passing test stale. Fix the test to tell the truth again, without deleting the coverage it protected.

Originate

No test exists yet. Turn acceptance criteria into failing tests, before any implementation, from the ticket alone.

Why split the role: a red test gives an implementer two ways to go green, change the code or change the test. Only one is legitimate. Separate the roles and every test change is a deliberate act by something whose only concern is whether the suite tells the truth.
11:00 – 12:30 · Verification

A Verifier Is a Floor, Not the Spec

A green checker is necessary. It is never sufficient. This holds for any of them.

  • A test suite, a linter, check_pod.py, a hand-written script: each proves a minimum bar
  • A floor checks fixed scenarios with known answers, not everything the ticket raises
  • Passing it with no other tests is not the same as being done
  • Naming what your judgment covers beyond it is part of the deliverable
  • If your tests don't cover more ground than the floor, that's a finding, not a pass
11:00 – 12:30 · Confirm Delegation

Two Paths, Then Measure the Payoff

Prove delegation works both ways, then check the context an isolated window actually saved you.

Proactive vs. explicit

Describe the task without naming the role. If Claude greps inline instead, the description is the bug. Then invoke it by name and compare: same result, guaranteed.

Isolation, measured

Check /context before and after delegating. The role's reasoning stays in its own window; only the summary crosses back. Don't take it on faith.

This is the orchestrator-worker pattern from Anthropic's multi-agent-systems writeup: the main conversation orchestrates, the subagent works in isolation. Lab 5 is where you measure the payoff, not just hear about it.
11:00 – 12:30 · One Working Tree

Fan Out Reads. Serialize Edits.

Subagents share one working tree, not private clones. That single fact sets the coordination rule.

Reads and reviews: fan out

Reading and reviewing parallelize for free. Point every role that only reads at the work at once.

Edits: one at a time

Two roles holding Edit at once overwrite each other, with no error. The loser's work is just gone.

Dependencies between steps and shared context are exactly what multi-agent handles worst. Serialize the six-file migration in dependency order, and decide deliberately whether the three sibling files are worth parallelizing.
11:00 – 12:30 · Put It Into Practice

Lab 5 Handoff

Two tickets, one arc: staff the pod, run WM-114 through it, then build WM-118 that didn't exist this morning.

WM-114 · investigate + migrate

StaffAuthor impact-mapper and release-scribe. Copy implementer, test-author, contract-reviewer from Lab 4. check_pod.py to 0.
InvestigateRun impact-mapper. Confirm it delegates unnamed, then by name. Ship impact_note.md.
MigrateBrief implementer to migrate six files bottom up. contract-reviewer checks for over-migration.

WM-118 · extend + document

ReframeThe stub's docstring is the whole spec. Decide what "changed" means before delegating.
Extendtest-author writes tests from your brief. implementer builds against them. impact-mapper sits out, on purpose.
Verifycheck_statement_delta.py is a floor. Name what your tests add on top.
The takeaway

The hand-off is the work. A role earns its place by the job it owns, and deciding a role doesn't apply is the same skill as deciding one does.

11:00 – 12:30 · Knowledge Check

Quick Check: Ship a Feature Through the Pod

1. Why must impact-mapper be copied nowhere, while implementer must be copied into this repo?

(a) impact-mapper is a smaller file

(b) impact-mapper is personal-scoped, already on your machine in every repo; implementer is project-scoped and doesn't follow you across repos

(c) Project-scoped roles can't be read-only

2. On WM-118, impact-mapper does no work. Why is that correct, not an oversight?

(a) WM-118 is too small to need a map

(b) WM-118 adds a new function and changes no existing signature, so there's no blast radius to trace

(c) impact-mapper only runs once per session

3. What is over-migration, and why does no test catch it by default?

(a) A caller you missed; the test suite always catches it

(b) Adding a parameter to a function that didn't need it (target_weights); every behavioral test still passes, so only an explicit reviewer criterion flags it

(c) Migrating files out of dependency order

4. Why must test-author write WM-118's tests, not implementer, and not from check_statement_delta.py?

(a) implementer isn't allowed to run tests

(b) A red test gives the implementer two ways to go green; and the checker is a floor, not the spec, so tests must originate from the ticket

(c) check_statement_delta.py already contains every test

11:00 – 12:30 · Recap

You Can Now...

  • Run the Read, Decide, Act, Observe loop twice on one feature, once per ticket, handing each pass to a different role.
  • Staff a pod across repos: author at personal scope, carry forward at project scope, and justify the difference as distribution, not capability.
  • Map a change's blast radius, direct, transitive, and not reached, and know that a direct-only map is wrong, not incomplete.
  • Migrate across files in dependency order, and catch over-migration: a signature changed that never needed to change.
  • Originate tests from a ticket before code exists, and decide when a role does not apply, defending the omission.
